newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco set for court fight vs. U.S. regulators.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco set for court fight vs. U.S. regulators.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent
The tobacco industry's key courtroom fight against federal regulation is set for Monday when manufacturers will argue that the Food and Drug Administration has no jurisdiction over cigarettes.

The long awaited oral arguments are scheduled before U.S. District Judge William Osteen Sr. in Greensboro, N.C., where the industry and other groups have sued to block the federal agency's proposed restrictions on the marketing and sale of cigarettes.
Joining tobacco companies as plaintiffs are the American Advertising Federation and the National Association of Convenience Stores.
The dispute stems from August 1995, when President Bill Clinton authorised the FDA to regulate how cigarettes are sold and marketed in a bid to curb smoking among children.

The FDA rules would ban free samples and billboard ads near schools and playgrounds, limit vending machine sales, ban sponsorship of sports events and the use of cigarette brands on hats, T-shirts and other products.
The rules would restrict advertising in some publications and require retailers to see picture identification for cigarette purchasers under 27 years old.
Unless blocked, the rules take effect in three phases. The first set, aimed at retailers, would take effect on Feb. 28, with the others due in August 1997 and August 1998.

Virginia, Kentucky and North Carolina, all major tobacco-growing states, have filed court papers urging the court to overturn the regulations. But at least 33 states, along with San Francisco and Guam, are supporting the rules.

The tobacco industry and other plaintiffs will present three main arguments during the hearing. They involve the intent of Congress concerning tobacco regulation, the language and legislative history of the Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act and First Amendment issues.

"We believe that each of these arguments is sufficient in and of themselves for the judge to rule that the FDA has acted unlawfully," Charles Blixt, senior vice president and general counsel of R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., told Reuters.
"Whether he rules on all three is up to the judge. Any one of them standing independently is sufficient to invalidate the rules," he said.

The first argument is expected to concern the plaintiffs' claim that Congress never gave the FDA the power to regulate tobacco and that the agency, by claiming jurisdiction, has bypassed lawmakers. The FDA has said in court papers that Congress has done nothing to deprive it of that authority.

The second argument will focus on language in the Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act, which provides for regulation of "drugs" and medical "devices." The tobacco industry says cigarettes do not fall under either of those categories.
Cigarette makers say the act's definition of device applies to products marketed for health reasons including medicine and surgical devices.

The FDA says cigarettes and smokeless tobacco are covered by the act because they are intended to affect the function or structure of the body. It also says new evidence shows nicotine is addictive and, therefore, the tobacco industry intends its products to be used for pharmacological purposes.

The last argument is the industry's claim that the ad restrictions violate the First Amendment since they are excessive and there are other ways to reduce smoking by young people besides restricting speech.
Many media lawyers including prominent First Amendment specialist Floyd Abrams have said it will be difficult for the FDA to convince courts the ad restrictions are constitutional.

But William Schultz, the FDA's deputy commissioner for policy, said direct action must be taken against tobacco ads. He said the limitations were narrowly tailored and did not ban all ads so were not excessive.
"I think we have a very strong record that promotion and advertising is a big piece of why kids smoke," he said.
